content: Multiple organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS) refers to a condition where multiple organ systems are affected either at the time of presentation or during the early stages of the disease. Examples of such diseases include systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), polyarteritis nodosa (PAN), sarcoidosis, diabetes, hypertension, metabolic syndrome, and acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). Regular eye examinations can play a critical role in identifying signs of systemic diseases. The eye is composed of various types of tissues, which makes it uniquely susceptible to a wide range of diseases. This anatomical complexity also allows the eye to provide valuable insights into the health of other body systems. Almost every part of the eye can reveal important diagnostic clues for systemic diseases. For instance, signs of systemic illness may be visible on the external structures of the eye, such as the eyelids, conjunctiva, and cornea, as well as in the middle and posterior segments of the eye, including the retina. Some researchers have also suggested that the physical condition of the fingernails and toenails can indicate the presence of systemic diseases. Careful examination of the nails may provide diagnostic clues, as certain systemic diseases are known to disrupt the nail growth process. The nail plate, which is the hard keratinized structure of the nail, is produced by the nail matrix located beneath the cuticle. As the nail grows, the distal portion of the matrix (closer to the exposed end of the nail) generates the deeper layers of the nail plate, while the proximal portion (closer to the base of the nail) forms the superficial layers. Any disruption in this growth process can result in changes to the nail's shape and texture. For example, nail pitting, which appears as small depressions in the hard surface of the nail, is commonly associated with psoriasis, affecting 10% to 50% of individuals with the condition. However, pitting can also be caused by a variety of systemic diseases, including Reiter's syndrome, other connective tissue disorders, sarcoidosis, pemphigus, alopecia areata, and incontinentia pigmenti. Additionally, conditions such as atopic dermatitis or chemical dermatitis, which interfere with the orderly growth of the nail matrix, can also lead to pitting.
